procedural_history.impugned_order: Award dated March 23, 1968, in Reference No. 39 of 1967
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Not mentioned in the provided text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by special leave by the workmen-appellants.

directions: There will be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the disciplinary proceedings were in contravention of the agreement arrived at on May 11, 1966, and therefore, the dismissal following such disciplinary proceedings amounted to unfair labour practice.

facts: Following a strike on May 11, 1966, an oral agreement was reached to end it.
The workers' association claimed this agreement included a promise from management not to take any disciplinary action against any worker in connection with the strike.
The management disputed this, arguing they only agreed not to victimize workers for simply participating in the strike.
The Labour Court heard conflicting evidence from both sides regarding the terms of this oral agreement.
law: The Supreme Court will not interfere with a finding of fact made by a lower court if that court has provided cogent reasons for its decision.
application: The Labour Court evaluated the evidence and held that the workers' association had failed to prove that the management agreed not to take any action against workmen in connection with the strike.
The Supreme Court treated the Labour Court's determination of the agreement's terms as a "finding of fact."
Since the Labour Court had provided cogent reasons for its finding, the Supreme Court decided not to interfere with it.
The Court also noted that the management did not, in fact, punish any workman solely for joining the strike.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, upholding the Labour Court's finding of fact that there was no proven agreement preventing the management from taking disciplinary action. Therefore, the disciplinary proceedings did not contravene the agreement and did not constitute an unfair labour practice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the orders of dismissal were illegal because they were passed on charges including intimidation, even though the enquiry officer did not find the misconduct of intimidation to be proven.

facts: The workmen were dismissed based on charges that included disorderly behaviour and intimidation.
The workmen argued that the dismissal was illegal because the enquiry officer did not explicitly find the charge of 'intimidation' to be proven in his report.
The enquiry officer's report stated that he accepted the management's evidence and that all charges against the workmen were proven.

The evidence that the enquiry officer accepted described the workmen's actions, such as thumping a hand on an officer's table, using threatening language (e.g., "you can see what we can do for you"), surrounding and pushing an officer, and trying to physically lift another officer from his chair.
application: The Court acknowledged that the enquiry officer did not use the specific word 'intimidation' in the summary of his findings.

However, the Court reasoned that the enquiry officer's acceptance of the evidence describing threatening and physically aggressive behaviour "must necessarily mean acceptance of the version of these officers that they were intimidated."
The Court concluded that the enquiry officer's finding of "disorderly behaviour" based on this specific evidence must be held to include the acts of intimidation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the workmen's contention. It held that the dismissal orders were not illegal because the misconduct of intimidation was effectively proven by the evidence that the enquiry officer accepted, even though the report did not use the specific term 'intimidation' in its summary.

issue.issue_text: Whether punishing only three workmen when a large number had participated in the strike constituted victimisation.

facts: A large number of workmen participated in a strike.
The management dismissed only three of these workmen.
Evidence from a domestic enquiry showed that these three workmen were at the forefront of a crowd that forced its way into a department.

The Court found that these three acted as leaders of the crowd and engaged in specific acts of incitement and riotous and disorderly behaviour, such as forcing officers to leave their desks and threatening them.
The management did not punish any workman, including the three concerned, for the act of simply participating in the strike. Action was taken only for the graver misconducts.
law: An act of discrimination can only occur if unequal treatment is meted out to those who are equally situated.
It is permissible for management to select those who led or misguided other workmen for disciplinary action.
If a misconduct graver than that of the rest is proven against specific workmen, punishing them for it cannot be considered victimisation.
application: The Court determined that the three dismissed workmen were not 'equally situated' with the other strikers because their misconduct was graver.
Their leadership role and specific acts of incitement and disorderly behaviour distinguished them from the general body of strikers.
The management was justified in taking a more serious view of the actions of these three workmen, who were the leaders.
Since the punishment was for these graver, distinct acts and not for the common act of striking, the action was not discriminatory or an act of victimisation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention that punishing only three workmen constituted victimisation. The Court reasoned that there was no discrimination because the three were not punished for simply striking, an act common to all, but for the graver misconduct of leading the crowd and engaging in incitement and disorderly behaviour. As they were not 'equally situated' with the other workers, singling them out for dismissal was justified.

issue.issue_text: Whether the findings of the enquiry officer were based on no evidence or were perverse.

facts.fact: During a domestic enquiry, management witnesses testified about the actions of three specific workmen.
relevant_text: The report of the enquiry officer against the said Vasudevan clearly stated that the enquiry officer accepted the evidence of the management's witnesses and that on that evidence all the charges against him stood proved.

facts.fact: Evidence showed one workman (Vasudevan) thumped a table and threatened an officer, saying "You can see what we can do for you now."
relevant_text: But the evidence which he, as aforesaid, accepted, was that Vasudevan along with other workmen entered the G. 2 department at about 3 P.M. on that day and thumping his hand on the table of the said Lakshman Rao threatened that officer in the following words : "now I am in the forefront [of the crowd]. You camnot do anything. You ask your people to come out and you also come out. Otherwise you can see what we can do for you now".

facts.fact: Testimony indicated that another workman (Prabhakar) was at the forefront of a crowd that squeezed and kicked an officer.
relevant_text: The evidence against Prabhakar was that he too was in the fore- front of that crowd which squeezed· Lakshman Rao and some members thereof inflicted kicks on him.

facts.fact: A third workman (Sandhyavoo) was identified as being in the forefront of the crowd and trying to physically lift an officer from his seat.
relevant_text: Similarly, there was the evidence of one Raja, the assistant personnel officer, and others that Sandhyavoo was one of those in the forefront of that crowd. According to Raja, Sandhyavoo tried to lift him from his seat with a view to force him to leave his tablo and finding that the crowd had become restive he left his place.

law.law_name: Standard of Review for Domestic Enquiry Findings
law.law_text: A court will not overturn the findings of a domestic enquiry unless they suffer from an infirmity, such as being based on no evidence or being perverse (a conclusion no reasonable person could reach based on the evidence).

application.explanation: The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence that was presented to the enquiry officer. It found that the enquiry officer had explicitly accepted the testimony of the management's witnesses regarding the specific, threatening, and disorderly actions of the three workmen.
relevant_text: Acceptamce of this evidence by the enquiry officer must necessarily mean acceptance of the version of these officers that they were intimidated by the crowd which forced its way into their department led by thes~ three work- men.

application.explanation: The Court determined that this accepted evidence directly supported the enquiry officer's findings of misconduct.
relevant_text: In our judgment the orders of dismissal, based on the findings in the domestic enquiry which did not suffer from any infinnity. could not be successfully impeached, and therefore, the Labour Coun was right in upholding them.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention that the enquiry officer's findings were based on no evidence or were perverse. It concluded there was "no substance" to this argument because the enquiry officer's report was based on specific evidence from management witnesses detailing the misconduct of the workmen. Therefore, the findings did not suffer from any infirmity and could not be successfully challenged.

issue.issue_text: Whether the strike was not illegal under s. 24 of the Industrial Disputes Act nor in contravention of any law as required by standing order 22(2) and (3).

facts: The workmen went on strike over the suspension of a fellow workman.
A settlement agreement was in operation at the time, which was binding on the workmen.
The workmen argued that the strike was not illegal because the reason for it (the suspension) was not a matter covered by the settlement agreement.
law: Under Section 24 (read with Section 23) of the Industrial Disputes Act, a strike is illegal if it concerns a matter covered by a settlement that is currently in operation.
Under Section 29 of the Act, a strike is illegal and punishable if it is in breach of any term of a binding settlement.
Standing Order 22 defines participating in a strike that is "in contravention of the provisions of any Act" or "any law" as misconduct.
application: The Court first determined that the strike was not illegal under Section 24 of the Act. This was because the reason for the strike—the suspension of a workman—was not a matter specifically covered by the settlement agreement.
However, the Court then considered whether the strike was illegal under any other provision of law.
It found that the strike was in direct contravention of a clause in the binding settlement.
A strike that breaches a binding settlement is illegal and punishable under Section 29 of the Act.
Because the strike was illegal under Section 29, it was a strike "in contravention of... any law" as described in Standing Order 22.
Therefore, participating in the strike constituted misconduct under Standing Order 22, which entitled the management to take disciplinary action.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that although the strike was not illegal under Section 24, it was illegal under Section 29 because it breached a binding settlement. This contravention of law meant that the strike constituted misconduct under Standing Order 22.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the disciplinary proceedings were in contravention of the agreement arrived at on May 11, 1966, and therefore, the dismissal following such disciplinary proceedings amounted to unfair labour practice.
appellant_arguments: The disciplinary proceedings and subsequent dismissals were a violation of the agreement reached on May 11, 1966, to end the strike.
This violation of the agreement constitutes an unfair labour practice.
respondent_arguments: The management did not agree to take no action against any workmen in connection with the strike.
The agreement was only not to victimise workmen for merely participating in the strike.
The management did not penalize anyone for simply joining the strike; the action was taken for other specific misconduct.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the orders of dismissal were illegal because they were passed on charges including intimidation, even though the enquiry officer did not find the misconduct of intimidation to be proven.
appellant_arguments: The dismissal orders were based on multiple charges, one of which was intimidation.
The enquiry officer found that the charge of intimidation was not proven.
Therefore, since the dismissal was based partly on an unproven charge, the entire order is illegal.
respondent_arguments: The dismissal was based on several charges of misconduct, not just intimidation.
The dismissal is valid as long as other serious charges were proven, even if the intimidation charge was not.

arguments.issue_text: Whether punishing only three workmen when a large number had participated in the strike constituted victimisation.
appellant_arguments: A large number of workmen participated in the strike and incited others to join.
Singling out and punishing only three of these workmen is an act of victimisation.
respondent_arguments: The three workmen were not punished for merely participating in the strike, but for specific and more serious acts of misconduct.
It is not victimisation to take action against the primary instigators or those who committed graver offenses, while not punishing the entire workforce.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the findings of the enquiry officer were based on no evidence or were perverse.
appellant_arguments: The findings of the enquiry officer were based on no evidence.
Alternatively, the findings were perverse, meaning no reasonable person could have reached such conclusions based on the evidence presented.
respondent_arguments: The enquiry officer's findings were based on the evidence presented during the enquiry and were not perverse.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the strike was not illegal under s. 24 of the Industrial Disputes Act nor in contravention of any law as required by standing order 22(2) and (3).
appellant_arguments: The strike was spontaneous and not illegal under section 24 of the Industrial Disputes Act.
The strike was not in contravention of any law as specified in the company's standing orders.
respondent_arguments: The strike was illegal under the Industrial Disputes Act and/or was in contravention of the standing orders.

cases.case_name: The Tata Engineering & Locomotive Co. Ltd. v. C. B. Mitter
cases.principle: A strike is illegal if it is in contravention of a binding settlement, even if it is not illegal under s. 24 of the Industrial Disputes Act. A clause in a settlement prohibiting strikes 'in no case' applies to strikes for any reason, not just those related to the subject matter of the settlement. Such a strike in contravention of the settlement is illegal under s. 29 of the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A settlement reached by a workers' association in its representative capacity is binding on the individual workmen. A strike by workmen in contravention of such a settlement is illegal, constitutes misconduct under the applicable standing orders, and entitles the management to take disciplinary action.
obiter: The Supreme Court will not interfere with a finding of fact made by a Labour Court when cogent reasons have been provided for it.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The strike was illegal not under s. 24 of the Industrial Disputes Act, but because it was a 'lightning one' resorted to without notice, in direct contravention of a binding settlement agreement between the management and the workmen. This illegality made participation in the strike a misconduct under the company's standing orders, thereby justifying the disciplinary action and subsequent dismissal of the workmen involved.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a strike is illegal due to its contravention of a binding settlement under s. 18(3) and s. 2(p) of the Industrial Disputes Act.
Whether participation in an illegal strike constitutes misconduct under the applicable company standing orders (Standing Order 22).
The standard of judicial review for a Labour Court's findings of fact, which the Supreme Court will not interfere with if cogent reasons are provided.
The standard for determining if an enquiry officer's findings are perverse or based on no evidence.
why_appellant_lost: The strike was found to be in breach of clause 5 of a binding settlement, which prohibited direct action without notice 'in no case'. The court reasoned the strike was 'a lightning one, was resorted to without notice and was not at the call of the association' and was therefore illegal.

The court deferred to the Labour Court's finding of fact that the management had not agreed to take no action against any workmen, but only 'not to victimise any workman for participating in the strike'. Since the management did not penalize anyone for merely joining the strike, there was no breach of agreement or unfair labour practice.
The claim of victimisation failed because the three workmen were not punished for merely participating in the strike, but for other specific and more serious acts of misconduct.
The court found there was 'no substance in the contention that the findings of tho enquiry officer were based on no evidence or were perverse.'
The challenge to the dismissal orders based on the unproven charge of intimidation was rejected, as other serious charges of misconduct were proven and were sufficient to justify the dismissal.
why_respondent_won: The settlement was binding on the workmen under s. 18(3) of the Industrial Disputes Act, and its prohibition of strikes without notice was absolute, as emphasized by the words 'in no case'.

Because the strike was illegal due to its contravention of the settlement, Standing Order 22 applied, which defined 'participating in or inciting others to join such a strike' as misconduct for which the management was entitled to take disciplinary action.

The management successfully demonstrated that it did not impose any penalty against any workman for simply joining the strike, thereby refuting the allegations of violating the May 11th agreement and engaging in unfair labour practice.
The Labour Court's finding of fact regarding the terms of the agreement to end the strike was upheld, as it was based on evidence and supported by cogent reasons.
policy_considerations: The court rejected the appellant's interpretation of the settlement because it 'would lead to a surprising result, namely, that though a strike at the instance of the association required four days' notice, a notice by the workmen without any call from the association would not require any such notice and that the settlement left complete liberty to the workmen to launch a sudden strike.' This upholds the sanctity and purpose of settlement agreements in maintaining industrial peace.
